video_title: When A.I. Spending Starts Slowing, Start Worrying About Recession | Wolf Richter
gist: Wolf Richter (wolfstreet.com) argues the US economy is running hot (Q2 nominal GDP +8.5%, ~6.4% inflation) as a deliberate White House/Fed strategy to erode the ~$40T federal debt, sees no near-term recession, and names an AI capex slowdown plus a major AI-stock sell-off as the likely future trigger. He rejects the K-shaped consumer narrative with credit data, locates affordability pain in housing and health insurance, and has exited stocks entirely in favor of TIPS and Treasuries while avoiding corporate/AI bonds and gold.

insights.claim: Wolf Richter says the US economy is running hot: Q2 nominal GDP grew at an 8.5% annualized rate with roughly 6.4% GDP-price inflation.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Nominal growth and inflation, not weakness, are the dominant macro regime per Richter.
insights.quote: nominal GDP without inflation, so that's the economic growth in current dollars was 8.5%

insights.claim: Richter argues the White House has chosen, and the Fed is going along with, a policy of high nominal growth and 3-5% inflation as the practical way to manage the ~$40 trillion federal debt, since no Congress will raise taxes or cut spending enough.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Expect persistently above-target inflation to be tolerated by policymakers.
insights.quote: the way to do this is with higher nominal economic growth and uh much higher uh inflation

insights.claim: Richter says the Fed still talks about a 2% inflation target but is effectively on the bandwagon of letting the economy run hot.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Fed rhetoric about 2% should be discounted versus actual tolerance of higher inflation.
insights.quote: the Fed's still talking about 2% inflation target, but they're really on the bandwagon, too

insights.claim: Richter predicts inflation will stay elevated in roughly the current range, making inflation (not growth) the main economic problem.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Position for sustained inflation rather than disinflation.
insights.quote: We're going to have uh inflation. Uh we already have inflation. It's quite a bit of inflation. It's going to stay up there in that range.

insights.claim: Because federal debt grew about 8% while nominal GDP grew 8.5% in Q2, the debt-to-GDP ratio falls, and since tax revenues track nominal GDP absent policy changes, interest expense becomes easier to cover.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Nominal growth outpacing debt growth is the key metric for fiscal sustainability.
insights.quote: when the economy outgrows the debt in current dollars, it it it yeah, it lowers the debt to GDP ratio, but it also GDP triggers taxes

insights.claim: Richter warns the run-hot strategy requires a fine balance: inflation of 20-30% would be catastrophic and would make investors unwilling to lend to the government.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Watch for inflation breaking out of the 3-5% band as the failure mode for bondholders.
insights.quote: if you have 20 or 25 or 30% inflation, that is a that is a catastrophic economic event

insights.claim: Richter says a recession would be magnified in this regime because falling nominal growth would compound normal recession problems with the debt problem, so policymakers are trying to avoid recession at all costs.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Expect aggressive policy response to any slowdown, with higher fiscal stakes.
insights.quote: if you have a recession and that thing goes down, you know, then we have a huge problem. It's magnified.

insights.claim: Richter lists the drivers of the hot economy: roughly $1 trillion of AI corporate and investor spending (much raised overseas), ~$2 trillion annual government deficits, full employment, rising wages, and wealthy stock-invested retirees spending.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Multiple simultaneous spending engines support nominal growth near term.
insights.quote: we've got the AI spending boom that's throwing maybe a trillion dollars in corporate money and investor money at the economy

themes.theme: AI capex as the recession trigger

insights.claim: Richter says a decline in AI investment spending, combined with a major sell-off in AI stocks, is the leading candidate trigger for the next US recession.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Track AI capex trends as the primary recession leading indicator.
insights.quote: When that starts declining uh that's when I start seeing a recession on the horizon.

insights.claim: Richter is not calling for a recession in the next couple of quarters; he sees no collapse in stocks or bonds and consumers remain employed.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Near-term macro base case is continued expansion.
insights.quote: I don't see I don't see any recession on the horizon.

insights.claim: Using the dot-com bust as a template, Richter notes the recession began about a year after the March 2000 sell-off started, because it took a large decline to destroy corporate confidence and trigger layoffs, cuts and project cancellations.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: After an AI-stock peak, expect roughly a one-year lag before recession.
insights.quote: it took 1 year during the dot-com bust from the beginning of the sell-off in March 2000, a year later the recession began

insights.claim: Richter says a 20% stock decline is not enough to cause a recession; it takes a much larger crash to eviscerate corporate willingness to spend.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Ordinary corrections should not be read as recession signals.
insights.quote: it's not a 20% decline, it takes a lot more and it takes uh a big stock market decline to to eviscerate corporate confidence in spending money

insights.claim: Richter expects a slowdown in AI spending would likely trigger the correction in AI stocks, with individual names potentially falling 80-90%.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Spending data may lead stock prices; concentrated AI holdings carry crash risk.
insights.quote: you can have these stocks go down by 80 or 90% and when that happens in your portfolio, you think, "Oh my god."

insights.claim: Richter says he has been wrong for a long time about how far the AI boom would go, explaining it by a constant global flow of hundreds of billions in debt, equity and IPO money into AI centers.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Capital inflows, not fundamentals, are sustaining the boom; watch the flow.
insights.quote: Well, I've been wrong about this stuff long enough. Uh I didn't think it would go this far. It keeps on going.

insights.claim: Richter judges an AI bust has a good chance of being worse than the dot-com bust because the current boom is shoving trillions of real money into the economy.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Downside scenario severity may exceed 2000-2002.
insights.quote: I think this is kind of a a good chance of being worse than the dot-com bust.

insights.claim: Richter expects an AI bust to hit concentrated tech hubs hard, with negative regional GDP heavy enough to drag national GDP and employment growth negative, while places like Tulsa may barely notice outside portfolios.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Regional exposure matters: tech-hub real estate and employment most vulnerable.
insights.quote: we may have negative GDP for for other places that is so negative and so heavily negative that it will drag down the national averages

insights.claim: Richter notes the data-center build-out spreads impact broadly: durable goods orders for power equipment such as gas turbines and on-site generators have skyrocketed, along with construction and power-line work that would stop when the boom ends.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Industrial and power-equipment suppliers are second-order AI-bust casualties.
insights.quote: We have seen uh durable goods orders for that kind of equipment skyrocket.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart notes AI-related companies are close to half of S&P 500 market cap and cites a Wall Street Journal chart showing AI investment as a share of GDP eclipsing prior tech revolutions including railroads.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Index concentration means an AI bust would not be contained like dot-com.
insights.quote: AI is is these companies are like almost half the S&P market value cap

insights.claim: Richter compares the AI build-out to the dot-com era's telecom/fiber-optic infrastructure wave (e.g., Lucent Technologies, broadband), which also involved massive global physical spending.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Infrastructure overbuild precedent suggests capex cycle risk.
insights.quote: lots of money was spent putting down uh fiber optic cables across the world

themes.theme: AI revenue model and deflationary pricing

insights.claim: Richter says the biggest problem of the AI bubble is an uncertain revenue model: consumers spend a fixed ~96-97% of income and cannot suddenly spend trillions more on AI.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: AI capex returns depend on revenue that may not materialize.
insights.quote: one of the the biggest problems this this bubble has is that the revenue model for AI is completely uncertain

insights.claim: Richter says companies are already curtailing AI spending and shifting to free models, producing super-deflationary, race-to-the-bottom pricing.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: AI model pricing power is weak; bearish for AI monetization assumptions.
insights.quote: it seems like the price the the the price models that are emerging are super deflationary

insights.claim: Richter's own consumer AI spend is limited to a few extra dollars per month from Google Workspace bundling Gemini, illustrating thin consumer monetization.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Bundling, not standalone subscriptions, is how consumers pay for AI.
insights.quote: I've got a uh uh an increase from from uh Google Workspace because now they include uh Gemini in it

insights.claim: Richter concludes there likely isn't enough revenue out there to pay for all the AI investments, a risk that is widely known yet ignored.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Known-but-ignored risk underpins eventual bust thesis.
insights.quote: there just isn't enough revenue out there in all likelihood to pay for all these AI investments

insights.claim: Richter says AI does raise productivity (he now makes his site's donation-ad graphics himself instead of hiring a designer; architects use it to cut workload), creating some labor substitution alongside AI-related hiring.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Labor impact is mixed: substitution in creative/services, hiring elsewhere.
insights.quote: I would have had to hire a graphic designer to do that. And that's where maybe where the the jobs impact comes in.

insights.claim: Richter rejects the K-shaped economy framing: the lower ~70% of households is not declining but rising more slowly than the top, and he told the New York Fed its own charts don't show a K.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Bearish consumer-collapse narratives may keep being wrong.
insights.quote: Your own charts show that one going up faster than the other but both going up.

insights.claim: Richter cites median married-couple household income of $128,000 as a cleaner measure than overall median household income, which is depressed by singles, students and asset-rich retirees on Social Security.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Headline median income understates the spending power of core households.
insights.quote: The typical that the median married couple household income is $128,000

insights.claim: Richter says corporate layoff announcements are largely a tactic to suppress wages and retention demands while companies such as Google and Amazon keep hiring.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Don't read layoff headlines as labor-market weakness.
insights.quote: this is a way for corporate America to bash down wages

insights.claim: Richter says roughly $7 trillion a year flows through US credit cards, with ~$1.3 trillion in statement balances but only about $500 billion of interest-bearing debt, growing perhaps $20 billion a year.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Credit card debt is a payment flow, not evidence of consumer stress.
insights.quote: It's half a trillion dollars. It's 500 billion, roughly.

insights.claim: Prime credit card delinquency is about 0.8%, near historic lows; overall card delinquency is about 2.8%, versus 6.5% in the financial crisis and over 4% in the early 2000s.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Credit metrics are normalizing from pandemic lows, not signaling crisis.
insights.quote: now we're at just below we're like 2.8%

insights.claim: Richter argues rising delinquencies are driven by higher-income borrowers (e.g., an overextended young dentist), since low-income people often can't get credit cards; subprime is a revolving status people fall into and climb out of.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Delinquency upticks reflect cyclical overextension, not low-income distress.
insights.quote: the people that have the most debt are the high-income people, and they're the ones that move the needle

insights.claim: Richter says subprime auto delinquencies spiked when lenders like Tricolor blew up (with some fraud), then came down; subprime is only ~15% of financed used-vehicle deals, and about half of used-vehicle deals are cash.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Subprime auto blowups are idiosyncratic and small in scope.
insights.quote: It's about 15% of the borrowing that goes on in the used vehicle market.

insights.claim: Richter says foreclosures have risen from near zero after pandemic bans but remain well below 2019 levels.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Housing credit stress is not elevated historically.
insights.quote: they have exploded from near zero, but they're still a lot below where they were in 2019

insights.claim: Richter calls University of Michigan consumer sentiment political hogwash because Democrat- and Republican-leaning respondents move in opposite directions.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Discount sentiment surveys versus hard spending data.
insights.quote: which tells you it's a political survey, not uh an economic survey

insights.claim: Richter says the real affordability crisis is in housing and health insurance, not everyday goods; high home prices cascade into higher insurance, property taxes, maintenance and HOA fees.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Affordability pain is concentrated in structural costs.
insights.quote: There is an affordability crisis, but it's in housing. It's in home purchases.

insights.claim: Richter says housing affordability can be restored without a crash via flat or falling home prices and rising wages, but it could take a decade or two; governments resist lower prices because they shrink tax revenue.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Expect a long, grinding real-price adjustment rather than a crash.
insights.quote: You don't have to have a housing crash to do that.

insights.claim: San Francisco home prices are spiking again on AI wealth (employees borrowing against illiquid stock), while some nearby Bay Area cities like Oakland are down about 25%.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: AI wealth effects are hyper-local; SF housing is a boom barometer.
insights.quote: Home prices are down 25% in some of those places. And um but not in San Francisco.

insights.claim: Richter argues housing affordability won't swing the midterms much because 65% of households own homes and like rising values.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Economic discontent may matter less politically than consensus expects.
insights.quote: 65% of the household own homes

themes.theme: Positioning: out of stocks, into TIPS and Treasuries

insights.claim: Richter is completely out of stocks, viewing the market as incredibly speculative.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: A notable macro voice is fully de-risked from equities.
insights.quote: I just think stocks are not for me. I'm out of it completely

insights.claim: Richter is unwinding his T-bill-and-chill position and buying TIPS, and participated in a recent 10-year note auction, seeing bonds as a valid investment for the first time in about 20 years.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Extending duration in Treasuries/TIPS at current yields is his preferred trade.
insights.quote: I'm unwinding my T-bill and chill and I've started buying uh uh tips

insights.claim: Richter is avoiding corporate bonds because spreads are still historically narrow and is staying '100 miles away' from AI bonds.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Credit spreads don't compensate risk; avoid AI-related debt.
insights.quote: I'm staying 100 miles away from AI bonds

insights.claim: Richter notes a 30-year Treasury bought in summer 2020 is down about 50% today, marking the end of the 40-year bond bull market that made bonds toxic.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Yields have reset enough to make long Treasuries modestly appealing.
insights.quote: if you bought a 30-year bond in in the summer of 2020 uh in in market trading today you're down about 50%

insights.claim: Richter warns of a dot-com-style bust pattern: indices fall 15-20%, investors hold and get rewarded, then fall another 20%, while individual stocks drop 80-90%.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Buy-the-dip conditioning can trap investors in a multi-leg bust.
insights.quote: stocks will go down 15% or 20% and people say, "Well, they went down 15% or 20% before, and I'll just hang on."

insights.claim: Richter sold his gold and silver, considers both still very high and vulnerable for traders, and would not buy at current prices.
insights.speaker: Wolf Richter
insights.so_what: Precious metals not attractive to him at current levels for trading.
insights.quote: I think it's still very high. I think it's still vulnerable. Same with silver.
